transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (NovaCore Head of ML), Samir Patel (Infra), Joan Reyes (Product)
body_transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, hope you can hear me okay. Uh quick roll call.
[00:00:06] Lena: Yep, I can hear you.
[00:00:08] Samir: I'm here. Sorry, on mobile.
[00:00:10] Maya: Great. Today's goal is a focused econ workshop for the pilot — dig into tokens-per-dollar, KV caching impact, and batching tradeoffs. Ethan will show the recent bench numbers.
[00:00:25] Ethan: Cool. I'll share my screen in a sec. Just to set expectations, these numbers are from the test harness we ran on the dedicated capacity nodes with 8g GPUs, quantized 4-bit profile. There are some noise factors but it should be representative.
[00:00:42] Joan: Quick question — when you say "tokens-per-dollar" are we comparing hosted rate card or the reserved/dedicated commit math?
[00:00:49] Maya: Good call. We'll show both: hosted API nominal cost and the committed dedicated per-hour node math converted into tokens per dollar for your workload.
[00:00:57] Ethan: Alright jumping into the data, first slide, baseline: no caching, synchronous inference, 1 request per connection. Average sequence length 180 tokens, prompt 80 tokens, generation 100 tokens. Throughput here is roughly 320 tokens/sec on the 8g profile, cost model uses our internal unit cost for quantized models.
[00:01:18] [00:01:22] Ethan: You'll see token cost under hosted is higher for small volumes but flattens at scale when we move to reserved nodes.
[00:01:30] Lena: That matches what we saw in our initial run. We care mostly about p95 latency — we have strict UX constraints of 500ms for short prompts.
[00:01:38] Ethan: Yeah for short prompts batching hurts latency. For 1-2 sentence calls batching is a tradeoff. With batching=8 we see tokens/sec improve ~2.8x but median latency jumps from 120ms to ~420ms. p95 goes up more.
[00:01:54] Samir: Is that with KV cache enabled?
[00:01:56] Ethan: No that's baseline without KV. With KV prefix caching and a hit rate around 45% for your trace, effective tokens/sec per dollar improves substantially — our estimate is ~1.6x better unit econ at 45% hit.
[00:02:10] Joan: The 45% hit number — where's that from? Our internal cache hits were lower in first week.
[00:02:15] Ethan: Right, that's from the toy dataset we used. We need your 7-day trace to align this. If your real workload has longer repeated system prompts and multi-turn patterns, hit rate could be 60-70%. If completely unique prompts per session it drops under 20%.
[00:02:32] Lena: Ok we'll share the trace — note that we redact PII.
[00:02:35] Maya: Perfect.
[00:02:36] [00:02:40] Ethan: Next I want to show a matrix for tokens/sec/$ across three configs: hosted (pay-per-use), dedicated reserved (monthly commit), and dedicated with aggressive quant + KV.
[00:02:50] Ethan: Hosted baseline 0.00012 tokens per dollar — that's a made-up unit in slide; dedicated reserved bumps to 0.00038, and dedicated+KV+quantization goes to 0.00066 in this workload.
[00:03:08] [00:03:12] Lena: So basically 5x improvement from hosted to dedicated+KV?
[00:03:15] Ethan: In that scenario yes, but it's workload dependent — key levers are prompt length distribution, cache hit, and batch size.
[00:03:22] Samir: On the infra side we worry about cold-starts and how KV cache persists. If we lose a node does the KV warm back up slowly?
[00:03:30] Ethan: Good point. KV is sharded in-memory per model shard; we can persist hot prefixes to a fast SSD-backed store and pre-warm on failover. There is some warm-up cost, we measured a 10‑15% transient hit on p95 for the first ~5 minutes during a scale event.
[00:03:48] Joan: That's okay if fallbacks are graceful. We need SLA for acceptable degrade window.
[00:03:52] Maya: We can include that in pilot SLOs for your dedicated nodes.
[00:03:55] [00:04:00] Ethan: Also important: batching policy. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLO guards. So we can set target p99 < 800ms and it will favor latency over throughput when necessary. But that reduces tokens/sec/$ because batches are smaller.
[00:04:16] Lena: Can you quantify the throughput drop when we enforce p95<500ms?
[00:04:20] Ethan: On this model it drops tokens/sec about 35% compared to unconstrained dynamic batching. So roughly tokens/sec/$ falls from 0.00066 to ~0.00043 in our table.
[00:04:31] Samir: Hmm that's sizeable. Our requirement is tight UI latency for search results, but background summarization could be cheaper. Is multi-route routing an option?
[00:04:38] Maya: Yes, route by interaction type — sync short prompts to low-latency pool, async long-running jobs to high-throughput reserved pool. We can do that in the pilot with simple header-based routing.
[00:04:50] [00:04:55] Ethan: We also experimented with quantization tuning; 4-bit vs 8-bit. 4-bit gives roughly 1.4x tokens/sec improvement but slight degradation in generation quality in edge cases. We have a recommended eval harness to measure quality delta; we can include that in the pilot so you can set an acceptance threshold.
[00:05:13] Joan: Quality threshold — what metric do you use? Perplexity? ROUGE? We need business metric like CTR or conversion impact.
[00:05:19] Ethan: Totally, we'll map model-level metrics (perplexity, exact match on tests) to your product metrics using your labeled eval set — part of the pilot deliverable.
[00:05:26] [00:05:30] Lena: On caching, one nuance — our sessions are multi-tenant and we can't leak prefixes across tenants. Is tenant-aware KV supported?
[00:05:37] Ethan: Yes, KV can be namespaced per tenant; hit rates will be lower if tenants are small, obviously. We can compute per-tenant econ to decide whether to shard by customer or global.
[00:05:47] Samir: We also ran into an error when trying to hit the private deployment earlier — it was a TLS issue with SNI. Might be our proxy.
[00:05:54] Maya: We'll include SE notes for network troubleshooting in the security doc we send.
[00:05:57] [00:06:02] Ethan: Jumping to the spreadsheet (shared link): column A is config, B is throughput tokens/sec, C is $/hour, D is tokens/sec/$, E is p95 latency. For your traffic sample we project dedicated+KV gives 2.1M extra tokens per dollar compared to hosted at your commit size.
[00:06:22] Lena: Can you explain the assumptions about tokenization? We use a different tokenizer sometimes that inflates tokens by ~1.12x.
[00:06:28] Ethan: Yes we used our baseline tokenizer; we'll re-run the bench with your tokenizer if you provide a sample. That directly scales tokens/sec/$ numbers.
[00:06:36] Joan: On pricing, what are the commit tiers? We need to know breakpoint for when dedicated is strictly cheaper.
[00:06:41] Maya: We have example tiers in the pricing doc. Roughly, for your traffic, commit at 3 nodes/month or more tends to favor dedicated. We'll send a tailored scenario.
[00:06:50] [00:06:55] Samir: Any concerns about model variant fallback? If we scale down or run out of capacity, is there an automatic fallback to a quantized or cheaper variant?
[00:07:02] Ethan: Yes, smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants — e.g., a 4-bit quantized variant or smaller parameter variant. There are quality tradeoffs and we can set automatic thresholds.
[00:07:12] Lena: Do you have guardrails so that fallback doesn't happen mid-session causing inconsistent outputs?
[00:07:16] Ethan: We can pin session-level model affinity for a session to avoid mid-session switch; for long sessions we can also have a re-eval window.
[00:07:23] [00:07:30] Maya: Let's talk next steps: We'll run the KV benchmark with your tokenizer and real trace. Ethan will instrument p95 and tokens/sec/$ across cache hit rates.
[00:07:38] Joan: Great. A couple of asks from our side: include a concrete cost calc example with 100k monthly users and 2 prompts per user, and show SSO/KMS integration steps.
[00:07:48] Maya: We'll include both in the deliverables.
[00:07:50] [00:07:55] Ethan: Quick FYI — we saw in one noise test that if you aggressively batch you can get 5x tokens/sec but latency becomes unusable for interactive flows, so the route-splitting approach is usually best.
[00:08:07] Samir: Noted. Also want to see the p95 warm-up curve when a node scales from 0 to 4 replicas.
[00:08:13] Ethan: We'll capture that in the 48-hour run.
[00:08:17] [00:08:22] Maya: Anything else on econ specifics?
[00:08:25] Lena: One more — do you charge for cache storage separately on dedicated?
[00:08:29] Ethan: Small charge for persisted SSD backing if you choose pre-warm persistence; in many pilots we absorb that or include it in the reserved node price. We'll call out the line-item.
[00:08:39] Joan: On security we need SOC2 scope, audit logs retention — is that configurable?
[00:08:44] Maya: Yes, SOC 2 is standard for dedicated/private; audit log retention is configurable and can be shipped to your SIEM.
[00:08:51] [00:08:56] Lena: Cool.
[00:08:58] Ethan: I'm going to note the bench parameters: 8g GPU, 4-bit quant, batch policy dynamic up to 32, kv persisted to ram+ssd, tokenizer baseline. Will re-run with NovaCore tokenizer and your trace.
[00:09:12] [00:09:30] Maya: Let's fast-forward to the end where we recap deliverables — Ethan will run the bench and share spreadsheet; Maya will send pricing; NovaCore will share traffic. We'll schedule security deep-dive next week.
[00:09:44] Joan: Works for me.
[00:09:46] Samir: Works.
[00:09:47] Lena: Fine.
[00:09:50] [00:09:55] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the links and action items.
[00:09:58] // (There was a short period of screen-share scrolling and some background noise)
[00:35:12] Ethan: (screen) I'm now showing the hit-rate sensitivity plot — x-axis is hit rate 0-100%, y-axis tokens/sec/$ normalized. See a sharp knee between 30-50% where econ improves rapidly.
[00:35:28] Lena: Our early data sits at ~28% so that explains why the numbers looked meh initially. If we can push to 45% with prompt templating it moves a lot.
[00:35:36] Joan: Is prompt templating something you help implement or is it on us?
[00:35:40] Maya: We can provide templates and a short playbook for increasing cacheability, part of the SE scope.
[00:35:45] [00:36:00] Samir: On networking, we also need to confirm the private deployment topology — are we using customer-managed VPC peering or a proxy?
[00:36:06] Ethan: Both supported. For strict compliance we recommend VPC peering/VPN with no NAT in the middle.
[00:36:12] Maya: I'll include network diagrams.
[00:36:15] [00:40:02] Joan: Quick tangent — what's the process for rolling model updates during pilot? We don't want sudden regressions in generation.
[00:40:08] Ethan: We support canary rollouts and eval gating; Redwood Optimize has regression alerts tied to prompt suites. We'll set an automatic rollback at X% quality drop.
[00:40:21] Lena: Good.
[00:40:25] [00:50:00] Maya: Recap and concrete next steps now, thanks again.
[00:50:08] Maya: Action items: Ethan run bench (due 3/25), Maya pricing (due 3/23), NovaCore share trace (due 3/24), Samir confirm network (due 3/22).
[00:50:20] Lena: We'll aim to get the trace by end of week.
[00:50:24] Joan: I'll compile prompts.
[00:50:27] Samir: I'll do the network inventory.
[00:50:30] Maya: Alright, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the security deep-dive on Tue 10am PT.
[00:50:36] Maya: Thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
[00:50:40] // call ends
